frontmatter.title: Model Comparison: Classifying Learning Strategies in the TAMBI Task

children.value: Participants in the TAMBI mosquito defense task face a complex learning problem: they must infer hidden environmental regularities - latent state transitions, cue-dependent directional offsets, and the distinction between noise and genuine change - from noisy, intermittent outcome feedback. Not all participants approach this problem in the same way. Some may engage in sophisticated latent structure inference, tracking hidden states and attributing surprises to their appropriate sources. Others may rely on simpler strategies: following the most recent outcome direction, or learning the association between cue colours and attack directions without ever building a model of the latent state dynamics. A small number may not engage meaningfully at all.

. This is essential for three reasons:

The four cognitive parameters (precision weighting, noise reactivity, belief momentum, perceived volatility) are defined within a latent-structure-learning agent. Estimating these parameters for a participant who is not performing structure learning would be scientifically inappropriate (analogous to fitting a linear regression model to non-linear data)

Participants who clicked randomly or without meaningful engagement should be identified and excluded from subsequent analyses. Here, model comparison provides an objective, data-driven exclusion criterion.
Characterisation of the learning strategy spectrum.

The distribution of winning models across participants provides insight into the prevalence of different learning strategies in the sample, and can be related to instruction condition and trait-level measures.

(Radev et al., 2023; Schmitt et al., 2023) to perform amortized Bayesian model comparison. The approach follows the same simulation-based inference logic as the parameter estimation pipeline: a neural classifier is trained on a large corpus of simulated behavioral data (generated from all candidate models), and then applied to real participant data to estimate posterior model probabilities.
The key advantage over traditional model comparison methods (e.g., BIC, AIC, Bayes factors via bridge sampling) is that amortized model comparison:
Operates on the same 40 behavioral summary features used for parameter estimation (ensuring consistency)
Provides well-calibrated posterior probabilities over models (not just point estimates or ranking)
Requires no per-participant optimization or sampling at inference time (~1 ms per participant)
Can be validated via confusion matrices, calibration curves, and model recovery analyses before application to real data

Rather than comparing a large number of models that differ in subtle ways, we define a compact set of five models that span the qualitative spectrum from disengaged behavior to full latent structure inference. This design reflects a principled ablation logic: each successive model adds a qualitatively distinct cognitive capability.

The rationale for limiting the set to these five models is twofold. First, the cognitive transitions they span (no learning → outcome tracking → cue association → multi-location coverage → latent structure inference) capture the most important qualitative distinctions in learning strategy. Second, model variants that differ only in continuous parameter settings within the structure-learning agent (e.g. with or without oddball attribution, with fixed or free volatility) are better handled by the parameter estimation pipeline, where these differences manifest as different parameter values rather than as discrete model classes. Maintaining them as separate models would constitute “double dipping” - testing the same cognitive dimension at both the model and parameter level.
The one model added beyond the original four, M_STRUCT4, deserves a word of justification because it does not introduce a new

of the task. A participant who has noticed that each cue is attacked from two structured directions could respond in two very different ways: by inferring which of the two hidden states is currently active and committing to it (M_STRUCT), or by simply covering both directions for each cue at once and never bothering to infer the current state (M_STRUCT4). Both look structured, and both are clearly distinct from single-direction tracking, but only the first is genuine latent-state inference. Without M_STRUCT4 in the set, a participant using the permanent-hedging strategy would be misassigned to M_STRUCT and counted, wrongly, as a structure-inferring learner. M_STRUCT4 exists precisely to absorb those participants and protect the interpretation of an M_STRUCT classification.
Participant exclusion criterion. Identifies data that are indistinguishable from random allocation.

On each trial, 7 nets are placed by drawing 7 slot indices uniformly at random (with replacement) from the 32 available slots. This produces allocations where each slot has approximately equal probability of receiving a net, with stochastic variation in the number of nets per slot due to the multinomial sampling.

2.5 M_STRUCT4: Four-Location Coverage Without State Inference

children.label: 2.5 M_STRUCT4: Four-Location Coverage Without State Inference

children.value: Distinguishes genuine latent-state inference from a structurally-aware but non-inferential strategy. This is the model that separates a participant who
the current hidden state from one who merely
all the structured locations at once.

The participant has discovered that each cue is associated with two structured attack directions - the two rotational positions of the hidden state - but does not infer which state is currently active. Instead of running a two-state HMM and committing to the inferred state, they permanently hedge fifty-fifty across both rotational modes for the current cue. Because the cues alternate, all four structured locations (two cues times two modes) remain continuously active across the session. Concretely, the model maintains up to two direction modes per cue via circular online

M_STRUCT4 never commits to a current state and never tracks transitions over time. Instead, it treats the task as a static four-location coverage problem; M_STRUCT treats it as a dynamic two-state inference problem. This is exactly the behavioural signature of the “permanent hedging” responders seen in the
, and giving that strategy its own model is what stops it from contaminating the M_STRUCT class.
The five models form a nested hierarchy of cognitive capabilities, with M_STRUCT4 sitting between cue-association and full state inference:

The key contrast the hierarchy makes visible is the one between the last two columns. M_STRUCT4 and M_STRUCT can both reproduce the four structured locations, so a participant who merely covers them is structurally indistinguishable from a state-inferrer on any static summary of
the nets go. What separates them is dynamics: whether the allocation

over time (M_STRUCT) or stays split across both modes throughout (M_STRUCT4). A participant classified as M_STRUCT is therefore not only producing structured allocations but is doing so in a way that is better captured by genuine state inference than by permanent coverage (even after accounting for the larger parameter count, since BayesFlow model comparison implicitly penalises model complexity via the prior predictive distribution).

For M_STRUCT specifically we check whether the classifier’s accuracy depend on the parameter values used to generate the data. This is central to evaluate whether some parameter regions produce behaviour that is indistinguishable from simpler models (and thus inducing identifyability issues). For example, M_STRUCT with very low noise reactivity and high belief momentum might resemble M_TRACK_CUE, because the agent rarely switches states. Conversely, M_STRUCT with very high h_switch might produce behaviour so variable that it resembles M_RANDOM.

We partition the parameter space into quintiles for each of the six M_STRUCT parameters and compute classification accuracy within each quintile. This identifies potential “blind spots” in the classification and informs the interpretation of boundary cases in real participant data.
However, this is not the case for our models as this figure shows.

The model comparison and parameter estimation pipelines are designed to be used sequentially:
Participants classified as M_STRUCT have their

Participants classified as M_TRACK_SIMPLE, M_TRACK_CUE or M_STRUCT4 are reported as using simpler strategies; their parameter estimates (if computed) should be interpreted with caution, as the structure-learning parameters (noise_reactivity, belief_momentum, h_switch) are not meaningful for agents that do not perform structure learning.
This sequential design ensures that cognitive parameters are only interpreted for participants whose behaviour is consistent with the generating model of those parameters.
